description: We are a multidisciplinary team of programmers and biotechnologists from Temuco, Chile, building software and scientific innovation for global and space challenges. We seek proactive, curious teammates who thrive under pressure and love bridging science and engineering—especially in frontend/full-stack development, biotechnology, UI/UX design, or data modeling. Above all, we value clear communication, ownership, and collaboration to turn ambitious ideas into working software.
summary: AstroHealth Guardian is an interactive web application that integrates astronaut health monitoring (HUMAN), spacecraft environmental parameters (SHIP), and gamified tracking of self-care habits and behavioral health (GARDEN). By combining crew health information, spacecraft telemetry in real time, and NASA scientific data, the platform translates the five spaceflight hazards identified by NASA’s Human Research Program into intuitive visual cues. Through an interactive human silhouette with color-coded organs, the application visualizes health indicators, explains how spaceflight hazards can affect physiological systems, and provides science-informed guidance for prevention and response to detected health anomalies or events. The GARDEN module, designed to support astronauts’ mental and emotional health, introduces a virtual plant as a metaphor for astronaut well-being: its appearance reflects the health status, its growth rewards self-care habits, and its surrounding weather represents the environmental conditions of the spacecraft. This integrated approach is essential because physiological, environmental, and psychological factors can interact and amplify health risks during spaceflight. By cross-referencing these elements, AstroHealth Guardian supports the early recognition of potential health anomalies, informed decision-making, and proactive health management, promoting crew autonomy and resilience during space missions.

Live Web App: https://jtapia07-crypto.github.io/astrohealth-spaceapps-2026/

✧ AstroHealth Guardian - "Body, mind, and spacecraft, united in a single system" ✧

How does it work?

AstroHealth Guardian operates as an interconnected monitoring and wellness ecosystem built around three synchronized modules:

  1. HUMAN – Astronaut Health Monitoring
  2. SHIP – Spacecraft Environmental and Operational Monitoring
  3. GARDEN – Personalized virtual plant (Mental Health and Gamified Self-Care)

1. Module HUMAN – Astronaut Health Monitoring:

Tracks health at both individual and crew levels. Each astronaut has an editable personalized profile containing medical history, allergies, baseline health indicators, and professional information. Selecting a profile displays that astronaut’s detailed health assessment, combining stored physiological baselines, recent self-reported health records, and simulated cabin telemetry.

An interactive body silhouette with color-coded nodes provides access to eight health monitoring organs/systems: head, eyes, heart, bones, muscles, blood, sweat, and saliva. Each one displays the current health status, an health score, relevant physiological and environmental indicators, Spaceflight Context explaining how spaceflight hazards can affect the corresponding physiological system, and General Actions on Board providing science-informed guidance for prevention, mitigation, and response.

A separate Crew Overview displays the general health status of all crew members, facilitating rapid access to important health information.

The How I Feel – Symptoms and Notes feature allows astronauts to record symptoms and personal health observations, displaying urgent escalation warnings when potentially serious symptoms are reported, such as chest pain.

When a potential health anomaly is detected, the alert management workflow displays the type of alert (Warning - red/Watch - yellow), potential causes, recommended actions, and guidance on contacting medical personnel. Alerts require acknowledgment and a documented resolution. The alert management workflow allows users to acknowledge alerts and mark them as resolved, supporting operational follow-up and event traceability. Through this, users can also flag alerts as potential false positives or non-emergency events, providing feedback that can support future refinement of the alert detection logic.

Finally, Historical Records maintain a traceable record of health-related events and documented responses.

2. Module SHIP – Spacecraft Environmental and Operational Monitoring:

Centralizes spacecraft status through an interactive spacecraft overview. The module combines simulated spacecraft telemetry with real-world space weather data retrieved through the NASA DONKI API, providing updated information on external spaceflight hazards. Its simulation panels and interactive controls for internal and external environmental conditions, as well as spacecraft operational parameters, allow users to explore adverse scenarios and visualize how different conditions can affect the spacecraft, astronaut health, and virtual garden. During each monitoring cycle, the system generates alerts according to the severity of detected anomalies or subsystem failures (CAUTION or CRITICAL). These alerts identify the affected parameter or subsystem, describe potential causes, provide recommended actions, and indicate when to contact mission control and follow authorized spacecraft procedures. As well as in the "HUMAN" module, the alert management workflow allows users to acknowledge alerts and mark them as resolved, supporting operational follow-up and event traceability.

3. Module GARDEN – Personalized virtual plant (Mental Health and Gamified Self-Care):

Features a personalized virtual and customizable plant selected from multiple available options, whose appearance, growth, and flowering reflect the astronaut’s health status and sustained self-care. Its surrounding environment is linked to spacecraft conditions and incorporates dynamic space weather information obtained through the NASA DONKI API. Designed to support astronauts’ mental health and emotional well-being during prolonged isolation and confinement, the gamified Daily Journal encourages healthy routines and self-reflection through positive reinforcement mechanisms, including accumulated points, daily points, current streaks, and best streaks. Astronauts can record everyday habits and well-being indicators, including sleep duration and quality, mood, stress, hydration, exercise, meals, and social interaction. The Wellness History feature tracks these records through daily, weekly, and monthly visualizations, supporting awareness of personal habits and changes in well-being over time.

(AstroHealth Guardian is designed for future integration with existing spacecraft sensors, biomedical monitoring devices, and wearable technologies, leveraging available infrastructure to enable automated data acquisition and continuous or periodic health monitoring.)

How did we use data and science:

The development of AstroHealth Guardian was grounded in NASA resources, astronaut biomedical datasets, technical standards, and peer-reviewed scientific literature to support the selection of health indicators, reference ranges, environmental parameters, and recommended actions.

  • Spaceflight hazards and health risks: NASA’s Human Research Program and Human Research Roadmap provided the scientific framework for understanding the five hazards of human spaceflight, their potential physiological and psychological effects, and associated countermeasures.
  • Biomedical and physiological data: NASA’s Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), through data like some of SpaceX Inspiration4 datasets, and the Space Omics and Medical Atlas (SOMA) provided scientific information on physiological, biochemical, cellular, and molecular changes associated with spaceflight.
  • Scientific literature: Peer-reviewed studies were consulted to support the selection and interpretation of health indicators, reference values, physiological responses, cognitive performance, and potential countermeasures.
  • Technical standards: NASA-STD-3001 (Human Factors, Habitability, and Environmental Health) served as a technical reference for spacecraft environmental conditions, habitability requirements, and crew health considerations.
  • Dynamic space weather data: The NASA DONKI API provides updated information on space weather events, integrating real-world data into the SHIP and GARDEN modules to contextualize external hazards and visualize their potential implications within simulated mission scenarios.

The platform combines these scientific resources with individual physiological baselines, self-reported health information, and simulated spacecraft telemetry to demonstrate an integrated approach to astronaut health assessment and environmental monitoring. Health scores and alerts are illustrative and are intended for health awareness and decision support rather than clinical diagnosis.

Benefits & Impact

  • Early recognition of health anomalies: Supports timely identification of potentially concerning physiological changes, enabling preventive and responsive actions before conditions worsen.
  • Holistic health management: Integrates physiological, psychological, and environmental information, facilitating a better understanding of their interdependencies.
  • Accessible health information: Simplifies the interpretation of complex scientific and medical data through intuitive visualizations, potentially reducing cognitive load.
  • Science-informed decision-making: Provides actionable recommendations for preventing and mitigating health risks and responding to detected anomalies or adverse events.
  • Mental health and emotional well-being: Encourages motivation, healthy habits, emotional awareness, and psychological resilience through gamification and positive reinforcement, particularly during prolonged isolation and confinement.
  • Greater crew autonomy: Supports proactive self-care and independent decision-making, particularly during long-duration missions with limited or delayed communication with Earth.
  • Potential terrestrial applications: Offers a scalable approach that could be adapted to isolated, confined, or extreme environments on Earth, such as Antarctic research stations.

Technologies and Tools

  • Consensus: scientific literature search and evidence-based research.
  • Replit: prototyping of page structure and front-end development of the web application (UX/UI).
  • Visual Studio Code: back-end development, with assistance from Claude (Anthropic) for refine and improve the project's source code.
  • JavaScript: implementation of interactive web functionalities.
  • HTML and CSS: web interface structure and styling.
  • JSON (JavaScript Object Notation): structured data representation and information exchange between application components.
  • TypeScript: type-safe programming to improve code reliability and maintainability.
  • Microsoft Excel/Google Sheets: data organization and definition of reference ranges for health indicators (based on published scientific literature and NASA data & resources).
  • ChatGPT (OpenAI) and Gemini (Google): as support for project structuring, information synthesis, writing, and translation.
  • ElevenLabs: to generate the voice-over narration for the project demo video.

(Note: AI tools helped accelerate the process, but the research, logic, direction, conceptualization and final solution were all led and developed by the team members.)

Creativity & Innovation

The creativity and innovation of AstroHealth Guardian lies in its integration of astronaut health monitoring, spacecraft environmental conditions, and a gamified self-care experience within a single personalized platform:

  • Purposeful gamification: One of our project’s most distinctive features is the personalized virtual plant that visually reflects the astronaut's health status, going beyond conventional data visualization by creating a symbolic and dynamic connection between astronauts, their health, and their habitat. This experience aims to foster self-care, emotional engagement, and mental and emotional well-being, especially in the context of isolation and confinement during space missions.
  • Multidimensional integration: Our platform integrates different health indicators and environmental data, recognizing that human health during space missions cannot be addressed in isolation from the conditions of the surrounding habitat. By bringing these dimensions together, AstroHealth Guardian provides a more holistic understanding of astronaut health, facilitating the interpretation of health indicators within their environmental context rather than as independent measurements. This reflects the core vision behind our platform: body, mind, and spacecraft, united in a single system.
  • Individual personalization: The platform recognizes that each astronaut has unique characteristics, health conditions, and responses to the challenges of spaceflight. By adapting the monitoring and self-care experience to each individual, we aimed to lay the groundwork for the future development of a personalized digital twin for each astronaut within our platform.
  • Collective health awareness and peer support: Through the Crew Overview feature, astronauts can access the general health status of their fellow crew members directly from their own profiles, without needing to log into other individual accounts. This promotes shared health awareness, facilitates the early recognition of potential health concerns among crew members, and supports timely peer assistance, particularly in situations where an affected astronaut may be unable to communicate their condition or request help.
